prompt:
Re-render image 1, the photograph, as a photograph taken on the surface of an airless world with its identical camera: the same position, height, direction and lens, every the horizon line and its hills, the boulder lower left and its shadow, the scatter of small rocks at the same place and size in the frame. The boulder is lower left, the open level plain centre-right, the sun low on the left so every shadow falls to the right. Nothing added to the airless plain under a black sky, no pulling back, no mirror image.

Image 1 is the photograph with simple grey stand-ins drawn where each cast piece goes. Image 2 is the rocket. Image 3 is the rover. Image 4 is the walker. Image 5 is the ringed planet. The stand-ins show only where; the pieces show what.

The rocket in image 2, exactly that rocket, landed upright on the open plain centre-right, its feet on the ground well below the horizon, its long shadow falling to the right, where image 1's stand-in outline is (x 0.52-0.66, y 0.16-0.60, about 44 percent of the frame height); keep its shape, colour and proportions, photographed in this light. The rover in image 3, exactly that rover, in the right foreground, driving away from the rocket and laying a cable across the ground, where image 1's stand-in outline is (x 0.66-0.84, y 0.58-0.84, about 26 percent of the frame height); keep its shape, colour and proportions, photographed in this light. The walker in image 4, exactly that walker, in the middle ground between the boulder and the rocket, planting core tubes, where image 1's stand-in outline is (x 0.38-0.50, y 0.60-0.77, about 17 percent of the frame height); keep its shape, colour and proportions, photographed in this light. The ringed planet in image 5, exactly that ringed planet, small and high in the black sky upper left, well above the horizon, lit from the left, where image 1's stand-in outline is (x 0.14-0.34, y 0.05-0.17, about 12 percent of the frame height); keep its shape, colour and proportions, photographed in this light.

A picture is ours when it is a wide, airless photograph of a grey regolith plain caught by a sun so low and so far to one side that every pebble pulls a long black shadow across the frame. The black sky sits in a thin band above a horizon cut as cleanly as ref 04's. A single dust-mantled boulder or crater lip holds a lower corner, as the solitary rock holds ref 11. A hard black terrain shadow, cast by a ridge we cannot see, breaks into the near foreground the way the photographer's shadow does in refs 02 and 17, except that it has the profile of the Moon and not a person. And in the lit middle distance there is a level, deliberate, empty pad of fine dust, laid out like a stage, waiting for a rocket that hasn't landed yet. Nothing on the ground has been touched: no print, no track, no object, no mark of the camera or the film.

Low sun from the left, a pure black starless sky, no air and no haze, razor-hard shadows; the rocket has just landed and the robots are already working.

Not the Apollo pastiche, not anyone at all, not the photographer's shadow, not hardware and flags, not foil, not left-behind things, not footprints and tracks, not kicked dust, not lettering, not the Earthrise sky, not haze and glow, not bonestell spires, not the Earth desert, not the CGI moon, not flat noon. No lettering except what this names.

Lock, repeated: the identical camera of image 1, boulder left, open plain right, sun left, every the horizon line and its hills, the boulder lower left and its shadow, the scatter of small rocks at the same place and size; the stand-ins become the pieces, nothing else is added to the airless plain under a black sky.
